title: Limits of classical mechanics

draft.title: Limits of classical mechanics
card: Classical mechanics is the physics of Newton. It predicts the motion of everyday objects very well, such as cars, balls and planets.
Classical mechanics assumes speeds simply add. A ball thrown forward at 10 m/s from a train moving at 30 m/s moves at 40 m/s relative to the ground.
At speeds close to the speed of light, this fails. Experiments show that fast particles do not behave as Newton's laws predict.
At everyday speeds, which are tiny compared with the speed of light, the error is too small to measure. So classical mechanics still works well there, and it is not wrong for cars or planets.
draft.remember: Newton's mechanics works at everyday speeds but fails for objects moving close to the speed of light.

a.q: Which situation is one where classical mechanics gives results that fail experimental tests?
opts: An electron moving at 99% of the speed of light
A cyclist riding at 15 m/s along a straight road
A spacecraft coasting at a few km/s past a planet
A footballer kicking a ball at 25 m/s across a field
a.why: Only the electron is moving close to the speed of light, where Newton's predictions fail. The other speeds are tiny compared with the speed of light, so classical mechanics works well. A spacecraft is fast by human standards, but still far too slow for the error to matter.
a.clue: Look for the speed that is close to the speed of light.

b.q: An engineer in Geelong designs a conveyor belt that carries boxes at 2 m/s. Why is classical mechanics suitable for this design?
opts: The speed is tiny compared with the speed of light
The boxes are heavy enough to avoid any error
Classical mechanics works for anything made of matter
The belt is on Earth, where relativity does not apply
b.why: At 2 m/s, the speed is far below the speed of light, so the error in Newton's predictions is too small to measure. Mass and location do not decide this. Relativity is not switched off on Earth, its effects are just tiny at low speeds.
b.clue: Compare the belt's speed with the speed of light.

a.best: An electron moving at 99% of the speed of light

b.best: The speed is tiny compared with the speed of light

problems.detail: The card says that at everyday speeds the relativistic error is 'too small to measure'. This is not strictly true. Time dilation has been measured at airliner speeds (Hafele-Keating) and even at about 10 m/s with optical clocks. Better wording: 'too small to matter' or 'negligible'.

Why (a) says a spacecraft at a few km/s is 'far too slow for the error to matter'. GPS satellites move at about 4 km/s, and their relativistic clock corrections do matter, which is point 5 of this chapter. This could confuse students later. Newtonian trajectories are fine at that speed, but the claim should be limited to the spacecraft's motion.
Why (b) repeats that the error at 2 m/s is 'too small to measure'. 'Too small to matter' would be accurate.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The card and the explanations say the relativistic error at everyday speeds is 'too small to measure', which is not strictly true. Why (a) also says the error does not matter at a few km/s, which clashes with the GPS corrections taught in point 5.
